channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Online communication with different types of friends can affect teens' mental well-being
item.description: In a study in Child and Adolescent Mental Health, researchers found that online communication with friends was associated with adolescents' mental well-being, but patterns varied by both frequency of communication and the type of friendship.

item.title: Supplement targeting aging processes shows potential to improve markers of blood vessel health
item.description: A multicomponent nutritional supplement has been found to improve markers of vascular health in a randomized controlled trial led by the University of Surrey. The formulation combined ingredients (vitamins, minerals, amino acids and plant-derived bioactives) selected for their relevance to several biological processes associated with aging.

item.title: Cannabis involved in most substance-related emergency visits among teens, young adults
item.description: A large national study analyzing emergency department visits and hospitalizations related to alcohol or cannabis use across the U.S. has found diverging age patterns: Among people who presented to the hospital for a substance-related problem, cannabis was involved in the majority of visits by adolescents and young adults, while alcohol predominated among older adults.

item.title: Hospital-acquired anemia common among ICU patients
item.description: Critically ill patients often develop anemia in the hospital, whether their hemoglobin levels are considered low upon admission or fall during their stay. Although seemingly minor compared to their other health issues, the blood loss is directly tied to a variety of poor patient outcomes.

item.title: Single dose of healthy liver vesicles may protect against alcohol damage
item.description: Alcohol-related liver disease (ALD) is characterized by hepatocellular injury, oxidative stress, inflammation and extracellular matrix remodeling, yet effective therapies remain limited. New research in The American Journal of Pathology, found that a single dose of liver matrix-bound nanovesicles (MBVs) derived from healthy porcine tissue reduced liver injury, fat accumulation and oxidative stress in alcohol-fed mice, pointing to a possible new therapeutic strategy for ALD.

item.title: Major changes discovered in medical profiles of adults diagnosed with autism since 2010
item.description: The medical profiles of adults diagnosed with autism have changed since 2010, finds a study of medical records in the U.K. and Sweden, published in the online journal BMJ Mental Health.

item.title: Large unexplained variation in emergency care hospital admission rates in England
item.description: Neither local case mix, primary care provision nor geography explains the large differences in hospital admission rates, ranging from less than 10% to more than 40%, from emergency departments across England, finds research published online in Emergency Medicine Journal.

item.title: How a gut virus hijacks mucus production to slip past the body's protective barrier
item.description: Among the various viruses that sicken your gut, some at least leave behind a tiny path of cellular destruction as they replicate, implicating the guilty pathogen. Both rotavirus and norovirus invade the small intestine, multiply there and can break through the organ's outer lining as one way of proliferating in the body.

item.title: Hidden ancestral links found in motor neuron disease and dementia could speed up gene discovery
item.description: Researchers at the Macquarie University Brain Institute and Clinic have helped accelerate the search for disease-causing genes by building new genetic 'families.' The team uncovered hundreds of previously unrecognized family connections by analyzing the DNA of people with frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and motor neuron disease (MND).

item.title: Recurrent visual field progression happens for 1 in 4 with glaucoma, study finds
item.description: Recurrent visual field progression after a first guided progression analysis (GPA) progression event is common, according to a study published online Oct. 22 in JAMA Ophthalmology.

item.title: Health system analysis reveals shift toward less invasive heart valve replacement among younger patients
item.description: New research simultaneously published in the Journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions and presented at TCT 2026 found that the annual number of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) procedures among patients younger than 70 increased nearly ninefold within one health system, rising from 15 in 2014 to 134 in 2024. Surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) remained the predominant approach across the age groups studied.

item.title: AI may help tailor treatment for childhood brain tumors
item.description: Choosing the right treatment for a child with a malignant brain tumor requires a careful balance. Therapy must be strong enough to keep the cancer from coming back, but it can also cause lasting side effects that affect learning, development and quality of life. Now, an international team led by researchers at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute has developed an artificial intelligence model that may help doctors make those decisions with greater precision.

item.title: Climate change is killing hundreds of thousands—a kidney specialist's concerns
item.description: The evidence that climate change threatens human health has never been stronger. Yet a new report suggests that world leaders are giving less attention to its health consequences in international political debate.

item.title: How a breast milk sugar supports infant gut development and prevents jaundice
item.description: A new study by researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine sheds light on the role of breast milk in supporting intestinal development and preventing hyperbilirubinemia, a condition in which bilirubin, a waste product from broken-down red blood cells, builds up in the blood and causes yellowing of the skin and eyes known as jaundice.

item.title: Blood signatures may explain roughly half of ultra-processed diets' links to heart disease and diabetes
item.description: Two distinct patterns of molecules in the blood linked to an ultra-processed diet and a minimally processed diet have been identified in a new study by UCL (University College London) and Imperial College London researchers.

item.title: AI-supported screening strategy could improve cervical cancer detection in low-resource settings
item.description: Combining HPV testing with artificial intelligence–based image analysis has shown efficacy in detecting precancerous lesions and guiding treatment decisions, according to a study led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal). The research, conducted within the HPV-Automated Visual Evaluation (PAVE) Consortium across nine countries, has been published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women's Health.

item.title: Women and men show similar short-term outcomes after aspiration thrombectomy for pulmonary embolism
item.description: New research presented at TCT 2026 found similar short-term outcomes in women and men with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) after aspiration thrombectomy, a catheter-based procedure to remove blood clots from arteries in the lungs, despite higher pretreatment risk among women. The results were simultaneously published in JSCAI.

item.title: Injectable glucose sensor component matches pricier alternative at one-tenth the cost
item.description: For millions of people living with diabetes, continuous glucose monitors provide a real-time picture of glucose levels, helping users manage medication, diet and day-to-day activities. But despite their benefits, the devices remain out of reach for some patients due to cost.

item.title: Breast cancer atlas reveals hidden subtypes to help chart course for precision oncology
item.description: A new molecular map of breast cancer has identified novel forms of the disease and provides a foundation for selecting personalized treatments guided by a tumor's molecular characteristics rather than standard pathology alone.

item.title: A possible chemical explanation for why we give up on tough tasks
item.description: When we engage our brains in a mentally taxing task, we eventually reach a point where we hit a wall or run on empty. Even when the rewards of finishing are obvious, we often find ourselves simply stopping. Exactly why this happens has long remained a mystery. We can easily point to tiredness or lack of motivation, but what is driving this disengagement at a biological level?

item.title: Food scores or warning labels? New study offers clues for Europe's nutrition labeling debate
item.description: A German–Israeli eye-tracking study found that both the design and familiarity of front-of-package nutrition labels shape what consumers notice and how they interpret food products. Participants in both countries found Israel's warning-label system easier to understand and more helpful for making healthy choices than Nutri-Score, offering timely evidence as Europe and the United States reconsider how nutrition information should appear on packaged foods.

item.title: Ultrathin optical coherence tomography endoscope could enable imaging during retinal surgery
item.description: A team of physicists from the Applied Optics Group at the University of Kent has developed a new design for an ultrathin, forward-viewing endoscope. Together with partners from King's College London and Moorfields Eye Hospital, they have engineered a device that captures optical coherence tomography (OCT) images of tissue up to about 1 mm beneath its surface. The initial prototype has a diameter of just 0.31 mm, small enough for potential use in retinal surgery.

item.title: New clues about why the eye's iris sheds in pigmentary glaucoma
item.description: Yale School of Medicine researchers have discovered new genetic risk factors associated with a subtype of the eye condition glaucoma. The findings highlight a novel mechanism that may contribute to the onset of the disease.

item.title: Postoperative complications elevated for patients with systemic lupus erythematosus
item.description: Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) have an increased risk for postoperative complications, according to a study published online Oct. 9 in Rheumatology International.

item.title: Newborn deaths fell by 50% in Flint following the launch of Rx Kids, new research finds
item.description: A new study published in JAMA Pediatrics has found that neonatal mortality—the death of an infant within the first 28 days of life—fell by 50% following the launch of Rx Kids, while early neonatal mortality—the death of an infant within the first seven days of life—fell by 74%.

item.title: Treatment satisfaction higher for patients with rheumatoid arthritis choosing their own treatment
item.description: For patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), those choosing their own treatment have higher treatment satisfaction, better treatment retention and fewer reported adverse events, according to a study published online Oct. 27 in RMD Open.

item.title: In the future, a blood test may be able to replace a biopsy
item.description: Doctors often have to take a tissue sample to understand what is happening inside a tumor or another affected organ. Biomedical scientist Danilo Mladenović is working to find the same information from a blood sample. Research carried out at Tallinn University may therefore help doctors detect diseases earlier and monitor treatment effectiveness without having to take repeated tissue samples.

item.title: A vulnerability in liver tumor cells' nuclear gateways could pave the way for new treatments
item.description: A study led by the Cell Cycle and Cancer Group at the Vall d'Hebron Institute of Oncology (VHIO) has identified a vulnerability in liver cancer that could guide the development of new therapies. The work, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, shows that some tumor cells depend on the combined action of two proteins, CDK16 and CDK18, to repair their DNA and continue multiplying. When both are inactivated, damage accumulates and the cells' ability to survive is impaired.

item.title: Fatty acid metabolism may help eliminate damaged and senescent cells
item.description: Researchers have identified a mechanism involving fatty acid metabolism that may determine whether a damaged cell enters senescence and persists in the body or is eliminated through cell death. Published in the journal Cell, the study could open new avenues for treating age-related diseases. Researchers from the University of Eastern Finland contributed to the international study.

item.title: Bad neighbors: How immune cells help cancer cells get ready to spread
item.description: Most cancer deaths are not caused by the original tumor, but by metastases, which form when cancer cells leave the original tumor and spread to other organs. To do so, cancer cells must loosen their attachment to other cancer cells and become more mobile so they can move away from the tumor, a process called epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, or EMT. EMT is a progressive phenomenon, and cancer cells go through an intermediate "hybrid" stage that is the best at forming metastases.
